items.summary: Dedicated meeting to discuss REP 0157: Wednesday, 4 November 2026 Hi everyone, At the ROS 2 PMC meeting on 27 October 2026 we discussed REP 0157 . There is a lot to cover, so the PMC agreed to hold a dedicated meeting on this REP. Anyone interested in REP 0157 is welcome to join. What is REP 0157? REP 0157 redesigns the rosidl messaging system so that ROS 2 gets native, universal zero-copy transport across process boundaries with minimal overhead. Key features: language-agnostic memory layouts, strict message constraints, and standardizing on XCDRv1 as the in-memory representation. Compatibility: designed to be backward compatible, with support for C, C++ and Python . Implementation: groups such as Ekumen-OS maintain experimental reference implementations and benchmarks to test constrained publisher and subscriber loans. items.title: String command and state interfaces in ros2_control
items.summary: Hello ros control friends. I have a issue here that I was looking to get opinions on: strings for command and state interfaces · Issue #3491 · ros-controls/ros2_control · GitHub Basically it is very common for us to have to read strings from the hardware devices that we support. Software/firmware versions are a big one. Checksums for interlocking, diagnostics and metrics, etc. I think using `control_msgs/msgs/GenericHardwareStatus` helps in some use cases. But I do feel there are some cases where we’d want the get a string from a device and map it into an existing message (like the battery state serial number). And in one case over the years at least, we needed to send commands to hardware using formatted strings. Now the implication of this is real time aspect of ros2_control. Though I feel there are lots of case for our application that isn’t “real time” per se. It just that the data follows the same pathway as everything else and it makes the most sense that it be natively supported in ros2_control. I’m curious if anyone else has this use case and if there are any existing solution people have come up with. 1 post - 1 participant Read full topic

Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. items.title: LLM Voice
items.articleText: LLM Voice 29 October 2026 Martin Fowler Sometimes when I read a post, I get the growing feeling that I'm reading the output of an LLM. I can't necessarily define why, although there are the common tells (it's not the em-dashes, it's the load-bearing tapestries). As I do this my desire to read on atrophies, sometimes to the point of revulsion There are tools out there that claim to be able to tell the difference between LLM-written prose and the old-fashioned biological product. I'm wary of them, partly due skeptism about their accuracy, but also because it rather misses the point. The reaction to LLM-Voice is a human one, that sense that we are in an uncanny valley of prose. By the time I'd reach for a tool to tell me what I'm reading, it's already too late, even if it confidently tells me there's no LLM present. I'm also suspicious of my own ability to accurately recognize LLM voice. Language changes over time, so a common sign of age is complaining about the language of the youngs. I'm inclined to bristle at prose that talks about “adopting a new sales motion ,” or “a sharp round-up of news”. But I've heard these constructs coming out of human mouths, so that's more a generational difference rather than between carbon and silicon. (And as a transplanted Brit, don't get me started on Americanisms, I'm sure I'll get used to them momentarily.) Right now I urge authors to be extra-wary of LLM-Voice. In particular I strongly recommend that authors should not fall into the trap of getting the LLM to write a draft. Even if it's edited by a human, it's very hard to expel the LLM-Voice - thus causing the uncanny valley reaction. 1 Even accepting suggestions of rephrasing is dangerous. I have heard of people using LLMs to develop outline and structure, that may be ok, but only as far as an outline. 2 Authors should fill the prose themselves. 1: Very hard, but not impossible. I've come across one case where I do know the first draft was entirely done by LLM, but I detected no LLM Voice when I read the final piece. It did, however, need a professional editor at a major periodical publication to clean it up. 2: My policy on this site, is that anyone who uses AI to help them write should declare how they used it, usually in the acknowledgments. This is partly for transparency, and partly so that readers can learn useful ways to use AI. In my own case, I don't use AI for generating prose, nor for help in structure. The only way I use it for writing is as a search tool (but I verify any information by going to the source). Say Your Writing is even more important in the age of LLMs. I habitually speak the words in my head and then write them down (and then edit what I've just written). This advice is particularly important to anyone who has any desire to communicate regularly with writing. Like many things, learning to be a good writer relies on lots of practice. It's a skill worth the time to acquire, but surrendering to an LLM will undermine any progress. In time it may be that LLMs will be so good that we can't tell the difference. In many ways, that's more worrying. Like most writers, I find writing an almost-essential tool for thinking. Often it's only by writing something down, that I can really get my thoughts on a topic into coherence. I've often started an essay knowing I don't really understand something, but the act of wrestling with the words forces me to overcome my confusions. As more people delegate writing to LLMs they will also delegate thinking and comprehension to LLMs. I don't want to do that, where's the fun of writing then? Although avoiding LLM-Voice is a general rule, it isn't an absolute one. An important example is that of Jim Highsmith (who contributes to this site). He finds working with an LLM is essential to his writing to overcome the bane of Parkinson's disease . I'll gladly deal with LLM-Voice in order to continue imbibing my old friend's wisdom. A more awkward case is that of translation. Many of my colleagues aren't comfortable in English, it is their second or fourth language. Some have found LLM translation an important part to their communication with those of us who know rather less Marathi. But I also would prefer rather a genuine human's clunky prose to the smooth but soulless LLM. There are situations where it would be reasonable for even a native Englishman to let LLMs write the prose. Such as if I'm writing a form letter to an official, or preparing a report I suspect no-one will ever read 3 . Maybe most documentation in the future will only be read by LLMs, and they won't have my uncanny valley worries. But if I want to communicate with humans, my humanity has to shine (or at least ooze) out of my prose. 3: Michael Nygard commented: “There you really aren't trying to communicate thoughts from one person to other people. You're communicating with a process rather than a human. A human may open the envelope but that person is acting as a component in a cybernetic organism.” Notes 1: Very hard, but not impossible. Claude Duet is the first personal-assistant-type harness that feels useful
items.articleText: Written by a human. Not affiliated with Anthropic. Look, I really didn’t want to like Duet. I don’t want to be an Anthropic fanboy and it annoys me when they do things better than the competition. But they have done it again. I have given serious effort to Muse, Dot, NanoClaw, and a host of other personal-assistant-type harnesses. Duet is the first one that felt more useful than tedious, and it feels like a serious evolution of the chat experience rather than another “give me all your credentials to be useful” agent. Here’s why I like it so far. 1. It’s fast Other assistant apps are always doing who-the-hell-knows-what in the background while I wait for a response. Duet clearly prioritizes getting a snappy response to the user even if background work is needed. It’s supposedly powered by Opus 5.5, but I’ve never seen Opus move this fast in other Claude UIs. Clearly some tuning went on here. This is critical to be a useful assistant: If you want to be my shell to the world, I am not going to sit and twiddle my thumbs between commands. 2. Channels are neat Maybe I’m just Slack-brained, but I really like Duet channels. In particular: I like that Duet can create and manage channels for me. One tedious aspect of working with LLMs is trying to keep track of chat sessions: workstreams get lost, context must be carefully maintained, sessions get misnamed, etc. Duet does the tedious session organizing for me. A natural hierarchy has emerged for my work, and I suspect I will have fewer lost threads with Duet. Cmd-k was already reflex for me: it pulls up the list of channels and lets me rapidly swap between them. Channels can also see and reference each other so Duet can help me keep work in the right lane. 3. Access policies are meaningful Access to Github repos is restricted per channel. I can add a few related repos to a specific channel, and not worry that the channel might commingle work from my other projects. It also never tries to get my credentials. This is my pet peeve with most assistant apps: they won’t do much until you hand them the keys. Muse has a credential store, which at least makes the agent blind to the values, but it could still enter those in something untrusted. Duet stores no credentials and actively discourages being given them. At best it might let you login via a Chrome session on its behalf. But it has never asked me to do that: it prefers to use the connector ecosystem Claude already has, and seems content to stay in its lane otherwise. 4. Responses are short This isn’t unique to Duet, Dot and Muse seem to get this too: Nobody wants to read a full page response to a simple question, which has been the de facto chatbot experience for years. I have always had to add a bunch of instructions trying to persuade my agents to give succinct responses. They all can also add emoji “reactions” to messages, though I find that personality makes a difference here: Muse tended to thumbs up everything, whereas Duet uses it to give me an okay without elaborating further, and I find that delightful. THAT BEING SAID It’s in beta, and definitely has some glitches. Sometimes threads are running but not visible. I’ve seen delegated repo access fail to attach correctly (race condition between agent start and access attachment?). I also acknowledge my use-cases likely make Duet a better fit for me in particular. Muse might be a better fit for others. YMMV. And Dot still reigns on voice interaction. Anthropic doesn’t even seem to care about having a conversational voice mode, it’s still just glorified speech-to-text. Duet is already replacing most of my AI workflows I don’t really enjoy the management side of managing agents: remembering who is running and with what context where. There is always some agent somewhere waiting on me to make a decision or follow up on some task. I’m sure some agent did brilliant work for me on a box somewhere that I’ve neglected and will be forgotten forever. The innovation that matters to me most is the hierarchy of concerns: The top level of Duet has a bird’s eye view of all my workstreams, but no low-level access. The channels carry more access, but under more constrained context. Sub-threads spun up by the channels can be even further constrained as they work in specific code sandboxes. The Desktop app can reach local hosts where I let it, and that’s usually only for the QA or deployment edge after the coding is done in the cloud. Most of this is how I already preferred to arrange my agents, and similar flows could be hacked together with some ducttape and API credits. Duet just makes this hierarchy a natural part of the core product, and it works so well that I suspect it’s going to be the default experience for all chatbot UIs in the near future. ← All posts

items.title: White House makes Section 232 determination regarding foreign-made robots
items.summary: The U.S. secretary of commerce's Section 232 investigation concluded that dependence on robotics imports poses a national security risk. The post White House makes Section 232 determination regarding foreign-made robots appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: A Section 232 investigation by the secretary of commerce found that robotics imports pose a threat to U.S. national security and economic competitiveness. Source: Office of the White House Yesterday, U.S. President Donald J. Trump issued a proclamation stating that the secretary of commerce had submitted a Section 232 report about the national security effects of imports of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as related parts and components. “Based on the facts considered in that investigation, and taking into account the close relation of the economic welfare of the Nation to our national security and other relevant factors, see section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), the Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that robotics, industrial machinery, and their components are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States,” stated the president. “Robotics and industrial machinery are critical to virtually all modern manufacturing processes, including for defense, commercial, and dual-use purposes,” he noted. “Furthermore, robotics and industrial machinery generate substantial economic value and support important economic activities, including approximately $7.1 trillion in shipments of manufactured goods in 2024 and the production of approximately $86 billion worth of equipment in 2024.” From mission-critical military and law-enforcement activities to critical infrastructure sectors such as agriculture , automotive , and electronics manufacturing , the U.S. government asserted that robots and related systems are vital to U.S. competitiveness. The value of such imported systems has grown over the past decade, and cybersecurity risks have also grown, according to the secretary of commerce. The Section 232 statement specifically cited “advanced robots — such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles” as providing direct support to the U.S. military. While investments in U.S. robotics production capacity have increased, they are not sufficient to meet U.S. demand, said the president. He directed the secretary and the U.S. trade representative to “to enter into negotiations with trading partners to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States.” Will this Section 232 determination lead to tariffs on foreign made robots? With most of the major industrial automation providers based overseas, it remains to be seen how trade negotiations will go. The threat of geopolitical rival China is motivating policies such as this investigation and recent FCC restrictions . Submit your innovation now! Experts expect Section 232 negotiations before any tariffs Industry leaders and observers offered initial reactions: “As I articulated last week on [a] panel at the Arrowfly RoboBusiness conference in Santa Clara with respect to the FCC action, this is another strong signal of government support for those working on developing and expanding domestic supply chains for robots,” Brendan Schulman, vice president of policy and government relations at Boston Dynamics , posted to LinkedIn . He noted that the Special Competitive Studies Project (SCSP ) Robotics Commission reached similar findings. “The next step for the federal government? Negotiations over the next six months with trading partners to adjust imports, and then further consideration of other trade policy measures,” added Schulman. “I am very pleased to see robotics gaining increasing attention and importance as one of the foundational technologies in need of broad, supportive policy action by the U.S. government. More to come, I’m sure!” Robert Little , former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc., 2026 Joseph F. Engerlberger Robotics Award honoree , and business development advisor, concurred. “Robotics are critical for any country rebuilding its manufacturing. I’m thinking, what took so long to make this a priority?” he told The Robot Report . “Today, we still have limited industrial robot manufacturing in the U.S.,” said Little. “Already, FANUC , Teradyne Robotics , and Yaskawa have announced investments aimed at expanding U.S. robot manufacturing. I expect more to come, and I hope this new proclamation helps accelerate it.” “Yet, what concerns me most are the gaps in our domestic supply of components for robotics and industrial machines: sensors, actuators, precision gears, encoders and more,” he noted. “We need a much stronger U.S. supply base for these components. This is where we need the most help to strengthen America’s ability to manufacture.” The Section 232 investigation does not mean that tariffs will be immediate, added Ash Sharma , vice president of research and chief information officer at Interact Analysis . “This shouldn’t be read as a new robotics tariff today, but it is a clear indication of the direction of travel,” he said. “The U.S. government has explicitly identified its reliance on imported robotics and industrial machinery as a national security concern and is seeking to strengthen domestic production,” commented Sharma. “If tariffs, quotas or other trade measures follow, they could have meaningful implications for supplier competitiveness, pricing, and manufacturing localization in the U.S., potentially affecting not just finished robots, but [also] the components that go into them.” The Robot Report is expecting more responses that will be shared in subsequent coverage. Panelists discussed reshoring and policies such as the Section 232 investigation at RoboBusiness 2026. Credit: Arrowfly About The Author Eugene Demaitre Eugene Demaitre is editorial director of the robotics group at Arrowfly (previously WTWH Media). He was senior editor of The Robot Report from 2019 to 2020 and editorial director of Robotics 24/7 from 2020 to 2023. Prior to working at Arrowfly, Demaitre was an editor at BNA (now part of Bloomberg), Computerworld, TechTarget, and Robotics Business Review. Demaitre has participated in robotics webcasts, podcasts, and conferences worldwide. He has a master's from the George Washington University and lives in the Boston area. Tell Us What You Think! items.articleText: This year, The Robot Report continued to share developments in design, engineering, and deployment of commercial systems, but the pace of change has accelerated. This is due to advances in hardware, scale, and most of all, artificial intelligence. The 2026 Robotics Handbook curates some of the top trends in the space. As labor shortages drive demand for automation, markets become more knowledgeable about robots’ capabilities, and the systems themselves get easier to use, robotics adoption is growing. According to the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) and the Association for Advancing Automation (A3), both global and U.S. orders are climbing after a post-pandemic pause. This free download looks at the engineering challenges, component choices, and market opportunities for robotics. While humanoid robots are still in development and commercial trials, massive amounts of funding have led to stiff competition as big tech companies and emerging startups try different form factors and use cases. AI is the other prominent topic of 2026, as it changes how robots are designed, programmed, and managed. From large language models and vision-language-action models to world models, AI is already starting to make robots more autonomous, easier to use, and safer for people to interact with. However, the devil is in the details, as concerns around data, cybersecurity, and national sovereignty persist. What the 2026 Robotics Handbook features The 2026 Robotics Handbook also looks at advances in dexterous manipulation and spotlights an industry where automation is just getting started — construction. In this issue, you can learn about: The importance of cost, humans in the loop, and generalization versus specialization of manipulators with Plus One Robotics What effects integration, safety, and the desire for human-level abilities have on the pace of humanoid development as seen in Jabil’s collaboration with Apptronik A look at how Boston Dynamics has approached end effectors as it works to bring its Atlas humanoid robot to market The role of “virtual gyms” and simulation to accelerate AI for complex robot behaviors from SoftServe Why suction and soft grippers are better than either alone with Locus Robotics How Monumental determined that bricklaying was the place to start with automation for the construction industry Sponsors for the 2026 Robotics Handbook include DigiKey , All Motion , CS Hyde Co. , Boker’s Inc. , SIKO Products Inc. , and ElectroCraft . items.title: AGIBOT introduces Worken to measure robot productivity at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026
items.summary: AGIBOT unveiled its AHA3 integrated platform, GO-3 Preview, and WITA-Omni 1.0 model, as well as the G2 Max robot and Link-U OS 1.0 framework. The post AGIBOT introduces Worken to measure robot productivity at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Peng Zhihui, president, CTO, and director of AGIBOT, introduces Worken at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026. Source: AGIBOT AGIBOT today introduced Worken, a proposed framework for measuring the productivity of robots in real-world environments, at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026 in Shanghai. Combining the words “Work” and “Token,” the concept seeks to shift attention beyond the number of robots manufactured or deployed toward how much useful work they can perform autonomously and consistently. The company also unveiled AHA3, its integrated “three intelligences in one” hardware platform, and highlighted advances in its AGILE motion intelligence framework, including a new self-evolving agent capability. AGIBOT debuted GO-3 Preview, its next-generation embodied AI foundation model, showcased its WITA-Omni 1.0 omni-modal interaction model, and launched the G2 Max industrial robot and Link-U OS 1.0. The event also featured actual applications across manufacturing and commercial services, demonstrating AGIBOT’s focus on translating robotics innovation into productive work. The company said they reflect its deployment-first focus, with practical innovation spanning robot hardware, locomotion, task and interaction intelligence, operations, and an ecosystem intended to support real-world deployment at scale. Founded in 2023 as Zhiyuan Xinchuang Technology Co., AGIBOT is focused on embodied AI. The Shanghai-based company ‘s portfolio spans humanoid robots, quadrupeds , dexterous systems, and commercial cleaning systems. Last month, AGIBOT said its 20,000th robot had rolled off the production line, and IDC reported that the company led global humanoid robot shipments in the first half of 2026. Submit your innovation now! Worken is a proposed measure of robot productivity As robots move from large-scale production into increasingly diverse applications, AGIBOT said there is another dimension of progress: the productive work robots can deliver once deployed. In addition to manufacturing scale, technological capabilities, and deployment milestones, the company said sustained autonomous operation and measurable task output are increasingly important indicators of robotic value. “Over the past few years, the robotics industry has made remarkable progress in hardware, AI models, and large-scale manufacturing,” stated Peng Zhihui, co-founder, president, and chief technology officer of AGIBOT. “But as robots begin working in factories, warehouses, and service environments, we need to answer a more practical question: How much productive work are they actually delivering?” “Worken is our attempt to develop a new way of answering that question,” he added. “We want to move beyond measuring how many robots are built or delivered and begin measuring how effectively they can perform useful work, autonomously and consistently, in the real world.” Even deployments involving similar numbers of robots can deliver different levels of productivity, depending on how independently the machines operate, how frequently human intervention is required and how much acceptable work they complete. AGIBOT described Worken as “effective intelligent work hours,” bringing three factors into a proposed measurement framework: Worken = Number of Active Robots × Autonomous Working Hours × Output Efficiency Ratio The first factor counts robots actively performing tasks in real-world environments, rather than units simply manufactured or held in inventory. The second measures time spent working autonomously, rather than total powered-on time. The third factor assesses productive output against a reference benchmark for a defined task, such as the amount of acceptable work completed by a human worker under established operating standards. The Worken framework combines the number of active robots, autonomous working hours, and an output efficiency ratio to measure robot productivity in real-world deployments. Source: AGIBOT By connecting deployment scale, autonomy, and task output in Worken, AGIBOT said it wants to provide a more comprehensive way to describe robotic productivity across applications such as industrial handling, logistics, inspection, and commercial services. “The concept also opens up a broader discussion about the economics of robotics,” said the company. “While hardware depreciates over time, improvements in software and AI models may enable the same machine to perform more useful work during its operating life. Measuring that output alongside total lifecycle costs could help businesses evaluate the longer-term value of robotic deployments.” AGIBOT said Worken is an evolving framework that will be further refined through deployments and operational data. By developing task-specific benchmarks and accumulating practical experience across different applications, the company said it hopes that Worken can serve as a widely applicable reference for measuring the productive value of physical AI. The event also featured the release of the “2026 Embodied Intelligence Industry Innovation Report,” which discussed the industry’s progress toward real-world deployment. Jointly compiled by China Economic Information Service and the Shanghai Industrial Innovation Center of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT ), the report included Worken and AGIBOT’s deployment examples as part of its industry analysis. AGIBOT unveils AHA3 platform and new physical AI models The AGIBOT Humanoid Architecture, or AHA3, which unifies “three intelligences in one” — locomotion, interaction, and manipulation Intelligence — in an embodied AI system. The company said it designed the third-generation hardware architecture to improve efficiency. Built on advances in motor-drive technology, integrated computing , and high-speed connectivity including Wi-Fi 6 and 5G, the AHA3 is designed to reduce integration complexity, improve system responsiveness, and support more capable robots in industrial applications. To support sustained industrial deployment, AGIBOT also introduced a joint liquid-cooling system intended to improve thermal performance during continuous operation, alongside specialized joints with IP67-rated protection for more demanding environments. Zhihui shows a hardware component of the AHA3 platform at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026. AGILE advances locomotion AGIBOT showed advances in its AGILE “multimodal, end-to-end locomotion intelligence” framework. The architecture spans general-purpose motion foundation models, generative motion control , integrated whole-body perception and control, and a newly introduced self-evolving agent capability. AGILE is designed to enable robots to explore the boundaries of their physical capabilities and progressively improve their performance through experience, extending motion intelligence beyond predefined behaviors toward greater autonomy and adaptability. AGIBOT described the framework as “a shift from motion control toward spatial mobility intelligence, with the goal of helping robots adapt to the layouts and changing conditions of real deployment sites.” A demonstration of task execution with GO-3 Preview, an embodied AI foundation model integrating reasoning, prediction, and action. Source: AGIBOT MEgo Glove and OmniHand get hands-on experience On the data side, AGIBOT introduced MEgo Glove, a wearable tactile data-collection device designed to capture human hand movements and contact information for training embodied AI models. Offered in Air and Ultra versions, the glove supports finger-pose capture, while the Ultra version adds three-dimensional fingertip and palm force data and torque information. The system is intended to help turn hands-on work experience into training data that can support robots after deployment. In addition, AGIBOT’s new dexterous hand family includes OmniHand 3 Lite, OmniHand 3 and OmniHand 3 Ultra, as well as the OmniPicker 3 tactile gripper , expanding the options for fine manipulation and task-specific deployment. The OmniHand robotic end effectors are designed for dexterous manipulation. Source: AGIBOT GO-3 Preview is built around WRAM AGIBOT also debuted GO-3 Preview, a next-generation embodied foundation model built around a World Reasoning Action Model (WRAM). The framework is designed to help robots anticipate the consequences of their actions, adapt to changing environments, and generalize beyond previously learned task sequences. The company also demonstrated zero-shot and few-shot capabilities and presented its approach to “physical intelligence scaling,” which combines pre-training and post-training with continuous improvement after deployment. This approach aims to enable robots to expand their capabilities through both structured training and experience gained from real-world operations. AGIBOT also highlighted GO-3 Preview’s benchmark performance. According to evaluation results presented at the event, the model ranked first in both task success rate and process score on RoboDojo, achieved the highest overall score on RoboTwin, and ranked first in overall score on RoboColiseum. These results demonstrate the model’s performance across multiple evaluation frameworks covering robotic manipulation and task execution. Across task and interaction intelligence, AGIBOT is seeking to connect data, models, robot hardware, and operating scenarios across pre-training, post-training, deployment and day-to-day operations. Feedback from real tasks can then inform subsequent improvements to models and workflows, creating a deployment-driven data flywheel. Dr. Yao Maoqing, co-founder, executive director, co-president, and president of the embodied AI business at AGIBOT, explains how GO-3 Preview and feedback from real-world deployments support the company’s data–model–robot–scenario learning loop. Source: AGIBOT WITA-Omni 1.0 integrates features for human-robot interaction For human-robot interaction, AGIBOT showcased WITA-Omni 1.0, an omni-modal foundation model that integrates visual perception, speech, real-time dialogue, facial expressions, and physical actions into a continuous interaction system. The model supports full-duplex conversation, coordinated speech and movement, and on-device deployment, enabling more natural and responsive communication in complex environments. WITA-Omni 1.0 currently ranks first on multiple benchmarks related to embodied interaction, including Daily-Omni. AGIBOT said AHA3, AGILE, GO-3 Preview and WITA-Omni 1.0 reflect its progress across integrated hardware architecture, locomotion intelligence, task execution and human-robot interaction. The company is also expanding its data collection, simulation and training capabilities through initiatives including AGIBOT WORLD 2026, the MEgo product family and Genie Sim 3.0, supporting the continued development of its physical AI models. This week, it also launched Genie Studio 2.0. Xiong Yan, partner, executive director, co-president, president of central R&D, and president of the interaction business at AGIBOT, presents WITA-Omni 1.0 and its planned deployment roadmap for more natural, multimodal human–robot interaction. Source: AGIBOT AGIBOT Launches G2 Max AGIBOT launched G2 Max, a heavy-duty industrial robot designed for manufacturing and logistics applications. Featuring 21 degrees of freedom, a dual-arm handling capacity of up to 40 kg (88 lb.) and an adjustable working height ranging from 0.1 to 2.5 m (0.3 to 8.2 ft.), the robot is built for demanding material-handling tasks. G2 Max’s force-controlled manipulation , omnidirectional mobility, and multiple safety features are intended to support efficient operations alongside existing industrial equipment and workflows. The G2 Max industrial robot features dual-arm handling, force-controlled manipulation, and omnidirectional mobility for manufacturing and logistics applications. entries.reason: 해외 로봇 및 부품 수입에 관한 미국 정부 차원의 안보 평가 결과와 향후 무역 정책 및 공급망 협상 방향을 다루어 산업적 영향이 큽니다.

facts.statement: 미국 상무부의 무역확장법 제232조 조사 결과 로봇, 산업 기계 및 부품 수입이 미국의 국가 안보를 저해할 위험이 있다고 판단되었다.
facts.quote: A Section 232 investigation by the secretary of commerce found that robotics imports pose a threat to U.S. national security and economic competitiveness.

facts.statement: 미국 대통령은 상무부 장관과 무역대표부(USTR)에 무역 파트너들과 수입량 조정을 위한 협상에 착수하도록 지시했다.
facts.quote: to enter into negotiations with trading partners to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States.

entries.title: AGIBOT, AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026에서 생산성 지표 Worken 및 하드웨어·모델 공개
entries.reason: AGIBOT이 제안한 로봇 생산성 측정 지표와 산업용 로봇 G2 Max, AHA3 플랫폼, GO-3 및 WITA-Omni 모델 등 포괄적인 기술 포트폴리오 발표 내용을 다룹니다.

facts.statement: AGIBOT은 활성 로봇 수, 자율 작업 시간, 출력 효율 비율을 곱해 로봇의 실제 생산성을 산출하는 Worken 지표를 제안했다.
facts.quote: Worken = Number of Active Robots × Autonomous Working Hours × Output Efficiency Ratio

facts.statement: AGIBOT은 AHA3 통합 하드웨어 플랫폼, 산업용 로봇 G2 Max, GO-3 Preview 및 WITA-Omni 1.0 모델을 함께 공개했다.
facts.quote: AGIBOT debuted GO-3 Preview, its next-generation embodied AI foundation model, showcased its WITA-Omni 1.0 omni-modal interaction model, and launched the G2 Max industrial robot and Link-U OS 1.0.

draft.section_industry: - **미국 상무부 무역확장법 232조 조사 결과 수입 로봇 안보 위험 판정**: 로봇, 산업 기계 및 부품 수입이 국가 안보를 저해할 위험이 있다는 조사 결과에 따라 무역 파트너들과 수입량 조정을 위한 협상 착수가 지시되었습니다 [16]. - **AGIBOT 생산성 지표 Worken 제안 및 신규 하드웨어·모델 공개**: 활성 로봇 수, 자율 작업 시간, 출력 효율 비율을 곱해 실제 생산성을 산출하는 Worken 지표를 제안하고, 산업용 로봇 G2 Max와 AHA3 하드웨어 플랫폼, GO-3 Preview 및 WITA-Omni 1.0 모델을 발표했습니다 [18].

findings: 수집일이 사건 발생일로 오인되지 않도록 본문에 명시된 2026-11-04 일정만 정확히 유지했습니다.

OpenAI의 API 크레딧 제공 조건($100, $200, $500 구독 플랜 대상)과 보도 주체 구분을 검증했습니다.
미국 상무부의 232조 조사 판정[16]과 중국 AGIBOT의 생산성 지표 및 상용 로봇 출시[18] 간의 상호 연관성을 도출하여 교차 분석(cross_insight)을 보강했습니다.

selectedItems.summary: Dedicated meeting to discuss REP 0157: Wednesday, 4 November 2026 Hi everyone, At the ROS 2 PMC meeting on 27 October 2026 we discussed REP 0157 . There is a lot to cover, so the PMC agreed to hold a dedicated meeting on this REP. Anyone interested in REP 0157 is welcome to join. What is REP 0157? REP 0157 redesigns the rosidl messaging system so that ROS 2 gets native, universal zero-copy transport across process boundaries with minimal overhead. Key features: language-agnostic memory layouts, strict message constraints, and standardizing on XCDRv1 as the in-memory representation. Compatibility: designed to be backward compatible, with support for C, C++ and Python . Implementation: groups such as Ekumen-OS maintain experimental reference implementations and benchmarks to test constrained publisher and subscriber loans. selectedItems.summary: The U.S. secretary of commerce's Section 232 investigation concluded that dependence on robotics imports poses a national security risk. The post White House makes Section 232 determination regarding foreign-made robots appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: A Section 232 investigation by the secretary of commerce found that robotics imports pose a threat to U.S. national security and economic competitiveness. Source: Office of the White House Yesterday, U.S. President Donald J. Trump issued a proclamation stating that the secretary of commerce had submitted a Section 232 report about the national security effects of imports of robotics and industrial machinery, as well as related parts and components. “Based on the facts considered in that investigation, and taking into account the close relation of the economic welfare of the Nation to our national security and other relevant factors, see section 232(d) (19 U.S.C. 1862(d)), the Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that robotics, industrial machinery, and their components are being imported into the United States in such quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States,” stated the president. “Robotics and industrial machinery are critical to virtually all modern manufacturing processes, including for defense, commercial, and dual-use purposes,” he noted. “Furthermore, robotics and industrial machinery generate substantial economic value and support important economic activities, including approximately $7.1 trillion in shipments of manufactured goods in 2024 and the production of approximately $86 billion worth of equipment in 2024.” From mission-critical military and law-enforcement activities to critical infrastructure sectors such as agriculture , automotive , and electronics manufacturing , the U.S. government asserted that robots and related systems are vital to U.S. competitiveness. The value of such imported systems has grown over the past decade, and cybersecurity risks have also grown, according to the secretary of commerce. The Section 232 statement specifically cited “advanced robots — such as autonomous robots, humanoid and quadruped robots, and autonomous ground vehicles” as providing direct support to the U.S. military. While investments in U.S. robotics production capacity have increased, they are not sufficient to meet U.S. demand, said the president. He directed the secretary and the U.S. trade representative to “to enter into negotiations with trading partners to adjust imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and their components so that such imports will not threaten to impair the national security of the United States.” Will this Section 232 determination lead to tariffs on foreign made robots? With most of the major industrial automation providers based overseas, it remains to be seen how trade negotiations will go. The threat of geopolitical rival China is motivating policies such as this investigation and recent FCC restrictions . Submit your innovation now! Experts expect Section 232 negotiations before any tariffs Industry leaders and observers offered initial reactions: “As I articulated last week on [a] panel at the Arrowfly RoboBusiness conference in Santa Clara with respect to the FCC action, this is another strong signal of government support for those working on developing and expanding domestic supply chains for robots,” Brendan Schulman, vice president of policy and government relations at Boston Dynamics , posted to LinkedIn . He noted that the Special Competitive Studies Project (SCSP ) Robotics Commission reached similar findings. “The next step for the federal government? Negotiations over the next six months with trading partners to adjust imports, and then further consideration of other trade policy measures,” added Schulman. “I am very pleased to see robotics gaining increasing attention and importance as one of the foundational technologies in need of broad, supportive policy action by the U.S. government. More to come, I’m sure!” Robert Little , former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc., 2026 Joseph F. Engerlberger Robotics Award honoree , and business development advisor, concurred. “Robotics are critical for any country rebuilding its manufacturing. I’m thinking, what took so long to make this a priority?” he told The Robot Report . “Today, we still have limited industrial robot manufacturing in the U.S.,” said Little. “Already, FANUC , Teradyne Robotics , and Yaskawa have announced investments aimed at expanding U.S. robot manufacturing. I expect more to come, and I hope this new proclamation helps accelerate it.” “Yet, what concerns me most are the gaps in our domestic supply of components for robotics and industrial machines: sensors, actuators, precision gears, encoders and more,” he noted. “We need a much stronger U.S. supply base for these components. This is where we need the most help to strengthen America’s ability to manufacture.” The Section 232 investigation does not mean that tariffs will be immediate, added Ash Sharma , vice president of research and chief information officer at Interact Analysis . “This shouldn’t be read as a new robotics tariff today, but it is a clear indication of the direction of travel,” he said. “The U.S. government has explicitly identified its reliance on imported robotics and industrial machinery as a national security concern and is seeking to strengthen domestic production,” commented Sharma. “If tariffs, quotas or other trade measures follow, they could have meaningful implications for supplier competitiveness, pricing, and manufacturing localization in the U.S., potentially affecting not just finished robots, but [also] the components that go into them.” The Robot Report is expecting more responses that will be shared in subsequent coverage. Panelists discussed reshoring and policies such as the Section 232 investigation at RoboBusiness 2026. selectedItems.title: AGIBOT introduces Worken to measure robot productivity at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026
selectedItems.summary: AGIBOT unveiled its AHA3 integrated platform, GO-3 Preview, and WITA-Omni 1.0 model, as well as the G2 Max robot and Link-U OS 1.0 framework. The post AGIBOT introduces Worken to measure robot productivity at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: Peng Zhihui, president, CTO, and director of AGIBOT, introduces Worken at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026. Source: AGIBOT AGIBOT today introduced Worken, a proposed framework for measuring the productivity of robots in real-world environments, at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026 in Shanghai. Combining the words “Work” and “Token,” the concept seeks to shift attention beyond the number of robots manufactured or deployed toward how much useful work they can perform autonomously and consistently. The company also unveiled AHA3, its integrated “three intelligences in one” hardware platform, and highlighted advances in its AGILE motion intelligence framework, including a new self-evolving agent capability. AGIBOT debuted GO-3 Preview, its next-generation embodied AI foundation model, showcased its WITA-Omni 1.0 omni-modal interaction model, and launched the G2 Max industrial robot and Link-U OS 1.0. The event also featured actual applications across manufacturing and commercial services, demonstrating AGIBOT’s focus on translating robotics innovation into productive work. The company said they reflect its deployment-first focus, with practical innovation spanning robot hardware, locomotion, task and interaction intelligence, operations, and an ecosystem intended to support real-world deployment at scale. Founded in 2023 as Zhiyuan Xinchuang Technology Co., AGIBOT is focused on embodied AI. The Shanghai-based company ‘s portfolio spans humanoid robots, quadrupeds , dexterous systems, and commercial cleaning systems. Last month, AGIBOT said its 20,000th robot had rolled off the production line, and IDC reported that the company led global humanoid robot shipments in the first half of 2026. Submit your innovation now! Worken is a proposed measure of robot productivity As robots move from large-scale production into increasingly diverse applications, AGIBOT said there is another dimension of progress: the productive work robots can deliver once deployed. In addition to manufacturing scale, technological capabilities, and deployment milestones, the company said sustained autonomous operation and measurable task output are increasingly important indicators of robotic value. “Over the past few years, the robotics industry has made remarkable progress in hardware, AI models, and large-scale manufacturing,” stated Peng Zhihui, co-founder, president, and chief technology officer of AGIBOT. “But as robots begin working in factories, warehouses, and service environments, we need to answer a more practical question: How much productive work are they actually delivering?” “Worken is our attempt to develop a new way of answering that question,” he added. “We want to move beyond measuring how many robots are built or delivered and begin measuring how effectively they can perform useful work, autonomously and consistently, in the real world.” Even deployments involving similar numbers of robots can deliver different levels of productivity, depending on how independently the machines operate, how frequently human intervention is required and how much acceptable work they complete. AGIBOT described Worken as “effective intelligent work hours,” bringing three factors into a proposed measurement framework: Worken = Number of Active Robots × Autonomous Working Hours × Output Efficiency Ratio The first factor counts robots actively performing tasks in real-world environments, rather than units simply manufactured or held in inventory. The second measures time spent working autonomously, rather than total powered-on time. The third factor assesses productive output against a reference benchmark for a defined task, such as the amount of acceptable work completed by a human worker under established operating standards. The Worken framework combines the number of active robots, autonomous working hours, and an output efficiency ratio to measure robot productivity in real-world deployments. Source: AGIBOT By connecting deployment scale, autonomy, and task output in Worken, AGIBOT said it wants to provide a more comprehensive way to describe robotic productivity across applications such as industrial handling, logistics, inspection, and commercial services. “The concept also opens up a broader discussion about the economics of robotics,” said the company. “While hardware depreciates over time, improvements in software and AI models may enable the same machine to perform more useful work during its operating life. Measuring that output alongside total lifecycle costs could help businesses evaluate the longer-term value of robotic deployments.” AGIBOT said Worken is an evolving framework that will be further refined through deployments and operational data. By developing task-specific benchmarks and accumulating practical experience across different applications, the company said it hopes that Worken can serve as a widely applicable reference for measuring the productive value of physical AI. The event also featured the release of the “2026 Embodied Intelligence Industry Innovation Report,” which discussed the industry’s progress toward real-world deployment. Jointly compiled by China Economic Information Service and the Shanghai Industrial Innovation Center of the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology (CAICT ), the report included Worken and AGIBOT’s deployment examples as part of its industry analysis. AGIBOT unveils AHA3 platform and new physical AI models The AGIBOT Humanoid Architecture, or AHA3, which unifies “three intelligences in one” — locomotion, interaction, and manipulation Intelligence — in an embodied AI system. The company said it designed the third-generation hardware architecture to improve efficiency. Built on advances in motor-drive technology, integrated computing , and high-speed connectivity including Wi-Fi 6 and 5G, the AHA3 is designed to reduce integration complexity, improve system responsiveness, and support more capable robots in industrial applications. To support sustained industrial deployment, AGIBOT also introduced a joint liquid-cooling system intended to improve thermal performance during continuous operation, alongside specialized joints with IP67-rated protection for more demanding environments. Zhihui shows a hardware component of the AHA3 platform at AGIBOT Innovation Day 2026. AGILE advances locomotion AGIBOT showed advances in its AGILE “multimodal, end-to-end locomotion intelligence” framework. The architecture spans general-purpose motion foundation models, generative motion control , integrated whole-body perception and control, and a newly introduced self-evolving agent capability. AGILE is designed to enable robots to explore the boundaries of their physical capabilities and progressively improve their performance through experience, extending motion intelligence beyond predefined behaviors toward greater autonomy and adaptability. AGIBOT described the framework as “a shift from motion control toward spatial mobility intelligence, with the goal of helping robots adapt to the layouts and changing conditions of real deployment sites.” A demonstration of task execution with GO-3 Preview, an embodied AI foundation model integrating reasoning, prediction, and action. Source: AGIBOT MEgo Glove and OmniHand get hands-on experience On the data side, AGIBOT introduced MEgo Glove, a wearable tactile data-collection device designed to capture human hand movements and contact information for training embodied AI models. Offered in Air and Ultra versions, the glove supports finger-pose capture, while the Ultra version adds three-dimensional fingertip and palm force data and torque information. The system is intended to help turn hands-on work experience into training data that can support robots after deployment. In addition, AGIBOT’s new dexterous hand family includes OmniHand 3 Lite, OmniHand 3 and OmniHand 3 Ultra, as well as the OmniPicker 3 tactile gripper , expanding the options for fine manipulation and task-specific deployment. The OmniHand robotic end effectors are designed for dexterous manipulation. Source: AGIBOT GO-3 Preview is built around WRAM AGIBOT also debuted GO-3 Preview, a next-generation embodied foundation model built around a World Reasoning Action Model (WRAM). The framework is designed to help robots anticipate the consequences of their actions, adapt to changing environments, and generalize beyond previously learned task sequences. The company also demonstrated zero-shot and few-shot capabilities and presented its approach to “physical intelligence scaling,” which combines pre-training and post-training with continuous improvement after deployment. This approach aims to enable robots to expand their capabilities through both structured training and experience gained from real-world operations. AGIBOT also highlighted GO-3 Preview’s benchmark performance. According to evaluation results presented at the event, the model ranked first in both task success rate and process score on RoboDojo, achieved the highest overall score on RoboTwin, and ranked first in overall score on RoboColiseum. These results demonstrate the model’s performance across multiple evaluation frameworks covering robotic manipulation and task execution. Across task and interaction intelligence, AGIBOT is seeking to connect data, models, robot hardware, and operating scenarios across pre-training, post-training, deployment and day-to-day operations. Feedback from real tasks can then inform subsequent improvements to models and workflows, creating a deployment-driven data flywheel. Dr. Yao Maoqing, co-founder, executive director, co-president, and president of the embodied AI business at AGIBOT, explains how GO-3 Preview and feedback from real-world deployments support the company’s data–model–robot–scenario learning loop. Source: AGIBOT WITA-Omni 1.0 integrates features for human-robot interaction For human-robot interaction, AGIBOT showcased WITA-Omni 1.0, an omni-modal foundation model that integrates visual perception, speech, real-time dialogue, facial expressions, and physical actions into a continuous interaction system. The model supports full-duplex conversation, coordinated speech and movement, and on-device deployment, enabling more natural and responsive communication in complex environments. WITA-Omni 1.0 currently ranks first on multiple benchmarks related to embodied interaction, including Daily-Omni. AGIBOT said AHA3, AGILE, GO-3 Preview and WITA-Omni 1.0 reflect its progress across integrated hardware architecture, locomotion intelligence, task execution and human-robot interaction. The company is also expanding its data collection, simulation and training capabilities through initiatives including AGIBOT WORLD 2026, the MEgo product family and Genie Sim 3.0, supporting the continued development of its physical AI models. This week, it also launched Genie Studio 2.0. Xiong Yan, partner, executive director, co-president, president of central R&D, and president of the interaction business at AGIBOT, presents WITA-Omni 1.0 and its planned deployment roadmap for more natural, multimodal human–robot interaction. Source: AGIBOT AGIBOT Launches G2 Max AGIBOT launched G2 Max, a heavy-duty industrial robot designed for manufacturing and logistics applications. Featuring 21 degrees of freedom, a dual-arm handling capacity of up to 40 kg (88 lb.) and an adjustable working height ranging from 0.1 to 2.5 m (0.3 to 8.2 ft.), the robot is built for demanding material-handling tasks. G2 Max’s force-controlled manipulation , omnidirectional mobility, and multiple safety features are intended to support efficient operations alongside existing industrial equipment and workflows. The G2 Max industrial robot features dual-arm handling, force-controlled manipulation, and omnidirectional mobility for manufacturing and logistics applications.
